forecasts.label: Capital financing requirement
forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Runnymede placed a moratorium on new borrowing for investment after a Best Value Notice in December 2023
news_drafts.lead:
Runnymede Borough Council "placed a moratorium on any new debt for investment" after it received a non-statutory Best Value Notice in December 2023, according to its second-quarter investment property update. The paper went to the Corporate Management Committee for its meeting on 19 November 2026.

The update says the notice raised concern over the council's high level of debt. It says the council has sought to reduce debt levels wherever possible.

The paper gives no figure for the council's debt or for the amount it has reduced it by.
news_drafts.paper_title: Final - CMC - Q2 Investment Property Update

news_drafts.headline: Runnymede took no new loans in first quarter, leaving £86.1m of its borrowing need met from its own cash
news_drafts.lead:
Runnymede Borough Council took out no new loans between April and June, paying for its capital spending from its own cash and reserves instead, according to its first-quarter treasury management report (how a council borrows, invests spare cash and manages the risks of both) to the Overview and Scrutiny Select Committee. Its total borrowing fell by £306,000 over the quarter, from £587.114m to £586.808m.

The council's capital financing requirement (the total it has spent on long-lived assets and not yet paid for, in effect its underlying need to borrow) stood at £672.931m. Borrowing of £586.808m left £86.123m of that need not covered by loans. The council held £89.1m in investments at the end of the quarter. The report says the council did not approach the Public Works Loan Board (the government's lending arm for councils) or the money markets.

The paper says the cash supporting the council's reserves, balances and cash flow was used "as an interim measure in the high interest rates environment and the period of low capital spend". It describes the approach as avoiding external borrowing costs while committing reserves to internal financing, which means using the council's own cash rather than taking a loan.
news_drafts.paper_title: 2026-27 Q1 Treasury Management Report v1 - Final

news_drafts.headline: Runnymede best value notice over high debt, issued December 2023, has been withdrawn
news_drafts.lead:
A government notice issued to Runnymede Borough Council in December 2023 over its level of debt has been withdrawn, according to papers before the Corporate Management Committee on 24 September 2026.

The Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government issued the non-statutory best value notice, a formal notice sent without using the department's legal powers. Its key comment cited concern over high debt. The committee's quarterly update on the council's investment property, the commercial property it owns to earn income, says: "Following the non-statutory best value notice, which has now been withdrawn."

The paper describes the council's response. It placed a moratorium on new investment debt, meaning no further borrowing to buy investment property, and pursued a strategy to reduce the debt it already held. The papers do not give the debt figures in this section.
news_drafts.paper_title: CMC - Q1 Investment Property Update - Final

findings.paper_title: Final - Appendices 1-5 - Fin Mon Report CMC Nov26
findings.headline: The general provision for inflation rises from £1,042k in 2027/28 to £4,188k in 2031/32.
findings.detail: The inflation provision is included in the net expenditure on services total. The paper gives the provision for each forecast year without itemising the assumptions.
findings.matters: A finance director can see how much of the medium-term budget gap is set aside for inflation, which is a common driver of the gap across councils.

findings.paper_title: Final - Appendices 1-5 - Fin Mon Report CMC Nov26
findings.headline: The Pay & Grading Review is shown at £1,241k in the forecast, rising to £1,279k and then £1,172k a year.
findings.detail: The line is tagged to the March 2026 Corporate Management Committee decision. The paper also records additional vacancy savings of £329k based on the first two quarters of activity.
findings.matters: A finance director can compare the recurring cost of a pay and grading review against the vacancy savings reported in the same period, which is a common pressure across councils.
findings.figures: £1,241k forecast in 2026/27; £1,279k in the following year; £1,172k a year thereafter; £329k additional vacancy savings

findings.paper_title: Final - Appendices 1-5 - Fin Mon Report CMC Nov26
findings.headline: Essential works arising from condition surveys of operational assets are shown at £245k, then £413k, then £1,578k a year.
findings.detail: The line is shown as zero in 2026/27 and rises across the forecast years. The paper does not link the figures to a specific capital programme or funding source in this table.
findings.matters: Finance officers at other councils with ageing operational estates can compare the scale of condition-survey work that is being built into the medium-term plan.
findings.figures: £245k; £413k; £1,578k in each of the following three years
findings.quote: Corporate Property - Essential works arising from condition surveys of operational assets 0 245 413 1,578 1,578 1,578

findings.paper_title: Final - Appendices 1-5 - Fin Mon Report CMC Nov26
findings.headline: An early repayment of a non-PWLB loan produced a £1,416k discount, transferred from the Financial Instruments reserve.
findings.detail: The paper also records capital financing savings from the early repayment of a non-PWLB loan of £228k in the current year and £1,057k in the following year. Treasury management income is reduced by £520k because lower funds are available following the same early repayment.
findings.matters: A lender or finance director can see the cost and saving from a debt repaid ahead of maturity, including the discount booked to reserve, which bears on the council's remaining debt profile.
findings.figures: £1,416k discount on loan repayment; £228k capital financing saving in the current year; £1,057k capital financing saving in the next year; £520k lower treasury management income
findings.quote: Discount on loan repayment transferred from Financial Instruments reserve (1,416) (1,416)

findings.paper_title: Final - Appendices 1-5 - Fin Mon Report CMC Nov26
findings.headline: The HRA capital programme shows slippage on the New Build Programme of £755k and £7,680k in the forecast columns.
findings.detail: The Appendix 5 table records slippage on the New Build Programme line, and the HRA working balance line records changes in use for capital expenditure of £7,680k in the forecast period. The paper also shows slippage on housing repairs capital of £3,064k.
findings.matters: Other councils' finance officers tracking HRA new build schemes can compare how far capital spend has been moved between years, which affects the timing of borrowing and reserve use.
